replace_in_block.new_heading: What's on a nut free catering menu?
new_paragraphs: Almost anything, rebuilt without nuts. A nut free menu in Dubai spans Mediterranean mezze, Italian pasta and risotto, Arabic grills, Indian curries, Asian stir-fries and modern European plates — the cuisine is your choice, the nut-free discipline is constant. The chef replaces nut oils with olive or sunflower oil, thickens sauces without ground almonds or cashews, and builds desserts around fruit, chocolate and dairy instead of praline, marzipan or frangipane. Nut free food catering in Dubai also means reading past the obvious: pesto, satay, some curry pastes, certain breads and many commercial cake mixes hide nuts, so the chef sources clean equivalents or makes them from scratch. You get a full tasting before the event to sign off on flavour and presentation, and the final menu lists every dish with its allergen status so nothing on the table is a guess.
How much does nut free catering cost in Dubai?

From AED 90 per person dropped off, AED 120 for a standard buffet and AED 150 with live stations. A private chef cooking and serving on site is AED 700 to 950 per person. Minimums are 10 guests on volume formats, 20 on a full buffet and AED 900 on order value, and set packages run from AED 1,200 per group.
Is there a surcharge for a nut free menu?
No. Allergen-aware sourcing and preparation are built into how the chef cooks, so a nut free menu is priced the same as any other catering menu at the equivalent format and guest count.
Can you cater for a severe, anaphylaxis-level nut allergy?

Menus without intentionally added nuts may be available on request. However, partner kitchens may handle nuts and other allergens, so cross-contact cannot be excluded unless specifically confirmed. The chefs we work with cook in your home or venue kitchen, so for an anaphylaxis-level allergy the precautions have to be reviewed and confirmed with you and the assigned culinary partner before you book.
What cuisines can be cooked without added nuts?

Most of them. Italian, Mediterranean, Arabic, Indian and Asian menus can all be built without intentionally added nuts, with nut oils, praline, marzipan and ground-nut thickeners swapped for alternatives.
What is included in the service?
From menu planning to the chef, the service staff, the plating and the cleanup — one team covers all of it, including clear allergen labelling on the day.
How do I book nut free catering in Dubai?
Share your date, guest count, venue and the nature of the allergy; we match a vetted chef and send an itemised proposal, usually within one business day.
For nut free catering, the chefs and partner kitchens handling your booking operate to Dubai Municipality food-safety requirements .

new_paragraphs: It covers the whole event, not just the cooking. A nut free catering company in Dubai handles menu design, ingredient sourcing, on-site cooking, service staff, plating, and full setup and cleanup — one team, start to finish. The chef reviews every recipe for tree nuts and peanuts, checks the labels on sauces, oils, spice blends, breads and desserts, and swaps out anything that carries a nut or a "may contain" warning. You confirm the guest count and the format you want; the chef confirms the menu and the precautions in writing. Because the food is prepared fresh for your event instead of pulled from a shared production line, there are fewer hidden ingredients to trace. That control is the whole point of a dedicated nut free caterer in Dubai: the person cooking your food is the same person who vetted every ingredient in it.

add_block.new_heading: What does nut free mean on a catering menu?
new_paragraphs: It means no tree nut and no peanut has been intentionally put into any dish on the menu — and the meaning is narrower than most people assume, which is why we agree it in writing before the chef shops. Tree nuts are almonds, cashews, pistachios, walnuts, hazelnuts, pecans, macadamias and Brazil nuts. Peanuts are not tree nuts at all; botanically they are legumes, grown underground, and a guest can react badly to one group while eating the other happily. Tell us which applies, because it changes what the chef has to avoid. Two ingredients that sound like nuts usually are not: nutmeg is a seed and coconut is a fruit, though plenty of allergy plans exclude coconut anyway and the chef simply follows whatever your specialist has written. Sesame and pine nuts are a separate brief again, and we treat them as one. The phrase to watch on a packet is "may contain nuts". That is a manufacturer saying the product shared a production line with nuts, not that nuts are in the recipe — for a mild sensitivity it may be acceptable, for an anaphylaxis-level allergy it usually is not, so tell us where your line sits and the chef sources around it.

add_block.new_heading: Desserts, cakes and dates — where the nuts actually hide
new_paragraphs: Dessert is where a nut free event most often comes undone, and in Dubai the dates on the table are the first thing to check. Stuffed dates are a fixture at almost every gathering here, and the filling is nearly always an almond, a pistachio or a walnut, so the chef serves nut free dates instead — plain Medjool and Khidri, or stuffed with candied orange peel, dried apricot or crystallised ginger, which look and eat like the real thing on a majlis platter. Arabic sweets need the same rework: baklava, maamoul and halva are built on pistachio, walnut or sesame paste, so they are either rebuilt or swapped for kunafa, basbousa, muhalabia or a fruit-led plate. The cake is the other trap, and it catches parents constantly. A cake bought from a bakery in Dubai will almost always carry a "may contain nuts" line, because the same room is decorating with praline, marzipan and frangipane an hour earlier, and no amount of asking at the counter changes what happened on that bench. So the chef bakes to order for your event rather than buying one in — a sponge, a ganache, a cheesecake or a pavlova made from ingredients checked one at a time, decorated without nut brittle or nut paste. If a child at the party also needs the dessert to be gluten free, say it at the briefing stage rather than on the day; our gluten free catering page explains how the two briefs are combined.

Tell us up front whether you are catering for a preference or a medical allergy — and if it is anaphylaxis-level, say so, because the precautions are more rigorous. The chef sources ingredients with no intentionally added nuts, prepares those dishes on cleaned surfaces with dedicated utensils to limit cross-contact, and labels each dish clearly at the buffet or on the plate. We are honest about the limits. Menus without intentionally added nuts may be available on request. However, partner kitchens may handle nuts and other allergens, so cross-contact cannot be excluded unless specifically confirmed. The chefs we work with cook in your home or venue kitchen, so for anaphylaxis-level allergies the exact precautions have to be reviewed and confirmed with you and the assigned culinary partner beforehand — we do not claim a completely nut-free environment without that agreement in place. Front-of-house staff are told what is in each dish and which items to keep separate, so no guest has to interrogate a waiter about their own dinner.
